It is said that the original was "hā'ukum," and the hamza replaced the kaf. Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of "hā'um" is "come here" (ta'ālaw).

Muqatil said: it means "halumma" (come), and it was said: "take" (khudhu). It is an ism fi'l (verb-noun), though it may be a plain verb when the attached pronouns of the plural subject are joined to it. It has three dialectal forms, as is known in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis). His saying "kitabiyah" is the object of "iqra'u" (read), because it is the nearer of the two verbs, and the object of "hā'um" is omitted, indicated by the object of "iqra'u." The estimated sense is: "Hā'um kitabiyah, iqra'u kitabiyah." The ha' in "kitabiyah," "hisabiyah," "sultaniyah," and "maliyah" is the ha' al-sakt (the pausal ha').

The majority (al-Jumhur) read these with the ha' kept both in pause and in continuous recitation, in conformity with the orthography of the Mushaf. Were it not for this, it would be dropped in continuous recitation, as is the case with the ha' al-sakt. Abu 'Ubayd preferred to deliberately pause on it, so as to agree with the language in attaching the ha' for pausing, and to agree with the script, meaning the script of the Mushaf. (p-1526)

Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Humayd, Mujahid, al-A'mash, and Ya'qub read it with the ha' omitted in continuous recitation and kept in pause, in all these words.

This reading is also transmitted from Hamzah, and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, following the language.

It is narrated from Ibn Muhaysin that he read it with the ha' omitted both in continuous recitation and in pause.

﴿Indeed, I thought that I would meet my reckoning﴾, i.e., I knew and was certain in the world that I would be called to account in the Hereafter. It was also said: the meaning is: "I thought that Allah would seize me for my sins, but He graciously pardoned me with His forgiveness and did not punish me."

al-Dahhak said: Every "zann" (thought/supposition) in the Qur'an from a believer is certainty (yaqin), and from an unbeliever it is doubt (shakk).

Mujahid said: The thought of the Hereafter is certainty, and the thought of this world is doubt.

al-Hasan said concerning this verse: The believer thought well of his Lord, so he did good deeds for the Hereafter, and the unbeliever thought ill of his Lord, so he did evil deeds.

It is said: The expression "thought" (zann) here is to indicate that what passes through the self of thoughts, which theoretical sciences generally do not escape, does not harm belief.

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾, i.e., in a praiseworthy life, not a disliked one, or one possessing contentment, i.e., its owner is content with it.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: "radiyah" means "marḍiyyah" (pleasing), like His saying: ﴿of a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 6], i.e., "mudfuq" (gushed). Thus what belongs to its owner is attributed to the life, and this is metaphor (majaz) in attribution.

﴿In a lofty garden﴾, i.e., elevated in place because it is in the heaven, or elevated in its dwellings, or great in souls.

﴿Its clusters are near﴾. "Qutuf" is the plural of "qitf" with a kasra on the qaf, meaning what is plucked from fruits; "qatf" with a fatha is the verbal noun, and "qataf" with a fatha or kasra is the time of plucking. The meaning is that its fruits are close to whoever reaches for them, whether standing, sitting, or lying down.

﴿"Eat and drink"﴾, i.e., it will be said to them in the Garden: "Eat and drink, with relish (hanian)," i.e., eating and drinking without any turbidity or disturbance. ﴿For what you sent forward in the past days﴾, i.e., because of the righteous deeds you put forward in the world.

Mujahid said: They are the days of fasting. As for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say, in grief and distress, because of what he sees in it of his evil deeds:

﴿"Oh, I wish I had not been given my record!"﴾, i.e., I wish I had not been given my record.

﴿"And I had not known what my reckoning is!"﴾, i.e., I did not know what my reckoning is, because all of it is against him.

﴿"Oh, I wish it had been the decisive end!"﴾, i.e., I wish the death I died had been the decisive one, and I had not been raised after it. The meaning of "al-qadiyah" is the one that cuts off life. The meaning is that he wishes for the permanence of death and the non-resurrection, when he witnesses the evil of his deeds and the punishment to which he will go. So the pronoun in "layta-ha" refers to the death he had died, though it is not mentioned, because, being so evident, it is as if it had been mentioned.

Qatadah said: He wished for death, and there was nothing in the world more hateful to him than it; and worse than death is that for which one seeks death.

It is also said: The pronoun refers to the state he witnessed upon reading the Book; the meaning: "Oh, I wish this state had been the death that was decreed upon me."

﴿"My wealth has not availed me"﴾, i.e., it did not repel from me any of Allah's punishment, whether "ma" is negative or interrogative; the meaning being: "What did my wealth avail me?"

﴿"My authority has perished from me"﴾, i.e., my proof has perished from me and gone astray from me. So said Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, and al-Dahhak.

Ibn Zayd said: It means my authority in the world, which is kingship. It was also said: my dominance over my limbs.

Muqatil said: It means when the limbs testified against him with polytheism.

And then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿"Seize him and shackle him"﴾, i.e., gather his hand to his neck with shackles.

﴿"Then burn him in the Blazing Fire"﴾, i.e., cause him to enter the Blazing Fire. The meaning is: do not burn him except in the Blazing Fire, which is the great fire.

﴿"Then insert him into a chain whose length is seventy cubits"﴾. The "silsilah" is a chain of linked rings, and its "dar'" (length) is its extent.

al-Hasan said: Allah knows with which cubit it is measured.

Nawf al-Shami said: Each cubit is seventy spans (ba'), and each span is farther than the distance between you and Makkah. Nawf was in the courtyard (rahbah) of Kufah.

Muqatil said: If one of its links were placed on the peak of a mountain, it would melt as lead melts. The meaning of "fasluk-uh" is "make him enter it," as one says "salaktuhu al-tariq," when one causes him to enter the road.

Sufyan said: We have been told that it enters through his rear until it comes out of his mouth.

al-Kalbi said: It threads him as a thread goes through pearls.

Suwayd ibn Abi Najih said: I have been told that all the people of the Fire are in that chain. The placing of the chain first is to indicate exclusivity, like the placing of the Blazing Fire.

The clause ﴿"Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty"﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) of what precedes it.

﴿"And did not urge the feeding of the needy"﴾, i.e., he did not urge feeding the needy from his wealth, or he did not urge others to feed them. The word "ta'am" (food) is placed in the position of "ik'am" (feeding), just as "'ata'" (gift) is placed in the position of "i'ta'" (giving), as the poet said:

"Kafran ba'da radd mawti 'anni wa ba'da 'ata'ika al-mal al-ri'aba?"
(Is it disbelief after my death was averted from me, and after your giving of abundant wealth?)

That is, after your giving. It is also permissible that "ta'am" retain its own meaning, not being placed in the position of the verbal noun, and the meaning is: he does not urge himself or others to give the very food of the needy. In making this the companion of abandoning belief in Allah, there is an exhortation to give charity to the needy and to meet their need, and an urging of oneself and people to that, which shows, in the most eloquent way and conveying the most complete benefit, that withholding it is among the greatest crimes and gravest sins.

﴿So there is not for him today here any close friend﴾, i.e., there will be no close relative for him on the Day of Resurrection in the Hereafter who benefits him or intercedes for him, because it is a day on which one flees from his close relative, and the beloved runs from his beloved.

﴿Nor any food except from ghislin﴾, i.e., he has no food to eat except the pus of the people of the Fire and what flows from their bodies of discharge and pus. "Ghislin" is "fi'lin" from "ghasl" (washing).

al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: It is a tree that the people of the Fire eat.

Qatadah said: It is the worst of foods.

Ibn Zayd said: No one knows what it is, nor what the zaqqum is, except Allah, Most High.

He, glorified be He, said in another place: ﴿They have no food except from *dari'*﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6]. So it is possible that *dari'* is *ghislin*. It was also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the meaning is: "So there is not for him today here any close friend except from ghislin," the *hamim* being boiling water. "Nor any food" means: they have no food they eat. There is no necessity for this inversion.

The clause ﴿"which none eat except the sinners"﴾ is an attribute of *ghislin*, and what is meant is the possessors of sins and the lords of transgressions.

al-Kalbi said: What is meant is polytheism.

The majority read *al-khati'un* with hamza, which is the active participle of *khati'a*, meaning one who does what is not right deliberately, while *al-mukhti'* is one who does it unintentionally.

al-Zuhri, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and al-Hasan read *al-khatiyun* with a damma on the *ya'* in place of the hamza.

Nafi' in one transmission read it with a damma on the *ta'* without hamza.

﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾. This is a rebuttal of the speech of the polytheists, as if He said: "The matter is not as you say," and "la" is extra (za'idah), the estimated sense being: "So I swear by what you witness and what you do not witness."

Qatadah said: He swore by all things, what is seen of them and what is not seen, so this includes all created beings. It was also said: "la" is not extra, but is for negating the oath, i.e., "I have no need of an oath because the truth in this is clear." The first view is preferred.

﴿Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger﴾, i.e., the Qur'an is indeed the recitation of a noble Messenger, with the meaning of "Messenger" being Muhammad ﷺ, or it is a speech conveyed by a noble Messenger.

al-Hasan, al-Kalbi, and Muqatil said: He means by it Jibril, and the evidence is His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger, possessor of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne﴾ [al-Takwir: 19–20]. In any case, the Qur'an is not the speech of Muhammad ﷺ, nor the speech of Jibril (peace be upon him), but it is the speech of Allah, so the estimation of "recitation" or "conveyance" is necessary.

﴿Nor is it the speech of a poet﴾, as you claim, because it is not among the kinds of poetry nor similar to it. ﴿Little is it that you believe﴾, i.e., you believe with little belief and confirm with slight confirmation, and "ma" is extra.

﴿Nor the speech of a soothsayer﴾, as you claim, for soothsaying is another matter with no common link between it and this. ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾, i.e., you remember a little, or you remember for a short time, and "ma" is extra. The paucity in both places is in the sense of negation, i.e., you do not believe and you do not remember at all.

﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. The majority read it in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is a revelation." Abu al-Sammak read it in the accusative as a verbal noun, with a verb omitted, i.e., "it was revealed as a revelation," and the meaning: "Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger, and it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds upon his tongue."

﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾, i.e., if that Messenger, who is Muhammad, or Jibril as previously mentioned, had fabricated. "Taqawwul" is the forced making of speech, and the meaning is: if he had forced that and brought it from his own self. Lying is called "taqawwul" because it is forced speech, and every liar forces what he lies about.

The majority read *taqawwala* in the active voice.

It is also read in the passive voice with *ba'd* in the nominative.

Ibn Dhakwan read *wa-law yaqul* in the imperfect form. *Al-aqawil* is the plural of *aqwal*, and *aqwal* is the plural of *qawl*.

﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾, i.e., by his right hand. Ibn Jarir said: This speech came in the manner of humiliation, according to the custom of people in seizing the one who is to be punished.

al-Farra', al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutaybah said: ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ means: with power and might. Ibn Qutaybah said: He placed the right hand in the position of power, because the strength of everything is in its right side, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Idha ma rayatun nusibat li-majdin, talaqqaha 'arabatu bi-l-yamin"
(When a banner is raised for glory, 'Arabah receives it with the right hand.)

And the saying of another:

"Wa lamma ra'aytu al-shams ashraqa nuruha, tanawaltu minha hajati bi-yamini"
(When I saw the sun shine its light, I took from it my need with my right hand.)

﴿Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾. The "watin" is a vein running along the back until it reaches the heart, and this is a depiction of his destruction in the most dreadful manner kings inflict on those they are angry with.

al-Wahidi said: The commentators say it is the nerve of the heart (niyat al-qalb). End of quotation. From this is the poet's saying:

"Idha ballaghtini wa hamalti rahli 'arabata fashriqi bi-dami al-watin"
(When you bring me and carry my saddle to 'Arabah, then choke on the blood of the aorta.)

﴿So none of you could prevent Us from him﴾, i.e., none of you would restrain Us from him or repel Us from him. So how would he fabricate lies against Allah for your sake, knowing that if he did so We would punish him, and you could not repel or restrain Us from him? "Hajizin" is an attribute of "ahad" (one), or the predicate of the Hijazi "ma."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 69, verses 19–52 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for the God-fearing.﴾ That is: the Qur'an is a reminder for the people of taqwa (God-consciousness), because they are the ones who benefit from it.

﴿And indeed, We know that among you are deniers.﴾ That is: some of you deny the Qur'an, and We will requite them for that. In this there is a severe warning.

﴿And indeed, it is a source of anguish for the disbelievers.﴾ That is: the Qur'an will be a source of regret and remorse for the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the reward of the believers. It was also said: it is their anguish in this world when they could not oppose it when they were challenged to produce a surah like it.

﴿And indeed, it is the certain truth.﴾ That is: the Qur'an, because it is from Allah, is true; so no doubt surrounds it, and no uncertainty reaches it.

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ That is: declare Him far above what does not befit Him. It was also said: pray to your Lord. The first is more appropriate.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Indeed, I thought﴾ that he said: "I was certain."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib concerning ﴿its fruits are near at hand﴾ that he said: "close."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Bara' concerning the verse that he said: "A man will take of its fruits while standing."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Then bind him﴾ that he said: "The chain enters his backside and comes out from his mouth, then they are strung on it as locusts are strung on a stick and then roasted."

Abu 'Ubayd, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-Darda' that he said: "Allah has a chain from which the cauldrons of the Fire have continued to boil since Allah created Hell until the Day it is placed around the necks of people. Allah has saved us from half of it through our faith in Allah, the Mighty. So feed the poor, O Umm al-Darda'."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the route of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Ghislin is the blood, the water and the pus that flows from their flesh."

al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "If a bucket of ghislin were poured out in this world, it would make the people of this world stink."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Ghislin is the name of a food of the people of the Fire."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him concerning ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾ that he said: "By what you see and what you do not see."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ that he said: "By power."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "The jugular (al-watayn) is the vein of the heart."

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated from him as well that he said: "The jugular is the nияt of the heart." (p. 1528)

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from him as well that he said: "It is the cord of the heart that is in the back."

﴿So there is not for him today here any close friend﴾, i.e., there will be no close relative for him on the Day of Resurrection in the Hereafter who benefits him or intercedes for him, because it is a day on which one flees from his close relative, and the beloved runs from his beloved.

﴿Nor any food except from ghislin﴾, i.e., he has no food to eat except the pus of the people of the Fire and what flows from their bodies of discharge and pus. "Ghislin" is "fi'lin" from "ghasl" (washing).

al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: It is a tree that the people of the Fire eat.

Qatadah said: It is the worst of foods.

Ibn Zayd said: No one knows what it is, nor what the zaqqum is, except Allah, Most High.

He, glorified be He, said in another place: ﴿They have no food except from *dari'*﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6]. So it is possible that *dari'* is *ghislin*. It was also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the meaning is: "So there is not for him today here any close friend except from ghislin," the *hamim* being boiling water. "Nor any food" means: they have no food they eat. There is no necessity for this inversion.

The clause ﴿"which none eat except the sinners"﴾ is an attribute of *ghislin*, and what is meant is the possessors of sins and the lords of transgressions.

al-Kalbi said: What is meant is polytheism.

The majority read *al-khati'un* with hamza, which is the active participle of *khati'a*, meaning one who does what is not right deliberately, while *al-mukhti'* is one who does it unintentionally.

al-Zuhri, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and al-Hasan read *al-khatiyun* with a damma on the *ya'* in place of the hamza.

Nafi' in one transmission read it with a damma on the *ta'* without hamza.

﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾. This is a rebuttal of the speech of the polytheists, as if He said: "The matter is not as you say," and "la" is extra (za'idah), the estimated sense being: "So I swear by what you witness and what you do not witness."

Qatadah said: He swore by all things, what is seen of them and what is not seen, so this includes all created beings. It was also said: "la" is not extra, but is for negating the oath, i.e., "I have no need of an oath because the truth in this is clear." The first view is preferred.

﴿Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger﴾, i.e., the Qur'an is indeed the recitation of a noble Messenger, with the meaning of "Messenger" being Muhammad ﷺ, or it is a speech conveyed by a noble Messenger.

al-Hasan, al-Kalbi, and Muqatil said: He means by it Jibril, and the evidence is His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger, possessor of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne﴾ [al-Takwir: 19–20]. In any case, the Qur'an is not the speech of Muhammad ﷺ, nor the speech of Jibril (peace be upon him), but it is the speech of Allah, so the estimation of "recitation" or "conveyance" is necessary.

﴿Nor is it the speech of a poet﴾, as you claim, because it is not among the kinds of poetry nor similar to it. ﴿Little is it that you believe﴾, i.e., you believe with little belief and confirm with slight confirmation, and "ma" is extra.

﴿Nor the speech of a soothsayer﴾, as you claim, for soothsaying is another matter with no common link between it and this. ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾, i.e., you remember a little, or you remember for a short time, and "ma" is extra. The paucity in both places is in the sense of negation, i.e., you do not believe and you do not remember at all.

﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. The majority read it in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is a revelation." Abu al-Sammak read it in the accusative as a verbal noun, with a verb omitted, i.e., "it was revealed as a revelation," and the meaning: "Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger, and it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds upon his tongue."

﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾, i.e., if that Messenger, who is Muhammad, or Jibril as previously mentioned, had fabricated. "Taqawwul" is the forced making of speech, and the meaning is: if he had forced that and brought it from his own self. Lying is called "taqawwul" because it is forced speech, and every liar forces what he lies about.

The majority read *taqawwala* in the active voice.

It is also read in the passive voice with *ba'd* in the nominative.

Ibn Dhakwan read *wa-law yaqul* in the imperfect form. *Al-aqawil* is the plural of *aqwal*, and *aqwal* is the plural of *qawl*.

﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾, i.e., by his right hand. Ibn Jarir said: This speech came in the manner of humiliation, according to the custom of people in seizing the one who is to be punished.

al-Farra', al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutaybah said: ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ means: with power and might. Ibn Qutaybah said: He placed the right hand in the position of power, because the strength of everything is in its right side, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Idha ma rayatun nusibat li-majdin, talaqqaha 'arabatu bi-l-yamin"
(When a banner is raised for glory, 'Arabah receives it with the right hand.)

And the saying of another:

"Wa lamma ra'aytu al-shams ashraqa nuruha, tanawaltu minha hajati bi-yamini"
(When I saw the sun shine its light, I took from it my need with my right hand.)

﴿Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾. The "watin" is a vein running along the back until it reaches the heart, and this is a depiction of his destruction in the most dreadful manner kings inflict on those they are angry with.

al-Wahidi said: The commentators say it is the nerve of the heart (niyat al-qalb). End of quotation. From this is the poet's saying:

"Idha ballaghtini wa hamalti rahli 'arabata fashriqi bi-dami al-watin"
(When you bring me and carry my saddle to 'Arabah, then choke on the blood of the aorta.)

﴿So none of you could prevent Us from him﴾, i.e., none of you would restrain Us from him or repel Us from him. So how would he fabricate lies against Allah for your sake, knowing that if he did so We would punish him, and you could not repel or restrain Us from him? "Hajizin" is an attribute of "ahad" (one), or the predicate of the Hijazi "ma."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 69, verses 19–52 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for the God-fearing.﴾ That is: the Qur'an is a reminder for the people of taqwa (God-consciousness), because they are the ones who benefit from it.

﴿And indeed, We know that among you are deniers.﴾ That is: some of you deny the Qur'an, and We will requite them for that. In this there is a severe warning.

﴿And indeed, it is a source of anguish for the disbelievers.﴾ That is: the Qur'an will be a source of regret and remorse for the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the reward of the believers. It was also said: it is their anguish in this world when they could not oppose it when they were challenged to produce a surah like it.

﴿And indeed, it is the certain truth.﴾ That is: the Qur'an, because it is from Allah, is true; so no doubt surrounds it, and no uncertainty reaches it.

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ That is: declare Him far above what does not befit Him. It was also said: pray to your Lord. The first is more appropriate.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Indeed, I thought﴾ that he said: "I was certain."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib concerning ﴿its fruits are near at hand﴾ that he said: "close."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Bara' concerning the verse that he said: "A man will take of its fruits while standing."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Then bind him﴾ that he said: "The chain enters his backside and comes out from his mouth, then they are strung on it as locusts are strung on a stick and then roasted."

Abu 'Ubayd, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-Darda' that he said: "Allah has a chain from which the cauldrons of the Fire have continued to boil since Allah created Hell until the Day it is placed around the necks of people. Allah has saved us from half of it through our faith in Allah, the Mighty. So feed the poor, O Umm al-Darda'."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the route of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Ghislin is the blood, the water and the pus that flows from their flesh."

al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "If a bucket of ghislin were poured out in this world, it would make the people of this world stink."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Ghislin is the name of a food of the people of the Fire."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him concerning ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾ that he said: "By what you see and what you do not see."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ that he said: "By power."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "The jugular (al-watayn) is the vein of the heart."

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated from him as well that he said: "The jugular is the nияt of the heart." (p. 1528)

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from him as well that he said: "It is the cord of the heart that is in the back."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 69, verse 19–52 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glorified be He, mentioned the Reckoning (al-'ard), He mentioned what will happen in it, so He said: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾, i.e., he is given his record which the scribes (al-hafaza) wrote down of his deeds, ﴿he will say, "Here, read my record!"﴾ He says this out of joy and delight.

Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Kisa'i said: The Arabs say: "ha, ya rajul" (hā, O man); for two it is "hā'uma, ya rajulan"; for the plural it is "hā'um, ya rijal" (O men). It is said that the original was "hā'ukum," and the hamza replaced the kaf. Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of "hā'um" is "come here" (ta'ālaw).

Muqatil said: it means "halumma" (come), and it was said: "take" (khudhu). It is an ism fi'l (verb-noun), though it may be a plain verb when the attached pronouns of the plural subject are joined to it. It has three dialectal forms, as is known in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis). His saying "kitabiyah" is the object of "iqra'u" (read), because it is the nearer of the two verbs, and the object of "hā'um" is omitted, indicated by the object of "iqra'u." The estimated sense is: "Hā'um kitabiyah, iqra'u kitabiyah." The ha' in "kitabiyah," "hisabiyah," "sultaniyah," and "maliyah" is the ha' al-sakt (the pausal ha').

The majority (al-Jumhur) read these with the ha' kept both in pause and in continuous recitation, in conformity with the orthography of the Mushaf. Were it not for this, it would be dropped in continuous recitation, as is the case with the ha' al-sakt. Abu 'Ubayd preferred to deliberately pause on it, so as to agree with the language in attaching the ha' for pausing, and to agree with the script, meaning the script of the Mushaf. (p-1526)

Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Humayd, Mujahid, al-A'mash, and Ya'qub read it with the ha' omitted in continuous recitation and kept in pause, in all these words.

This reading is also transmitted from Hamzah, and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, following the language.

It is narrated from Ibn Muhaysin that he read it with the ha' omitted both in continuous recitation and in pause.

﴿Indeed, I thought that I would meet my reckoning﴾, i.e., I knew and was certain in the world that I would be called to account in the Hereafter. It was also said: the meaning is: "I thought that Allah would seize me for my sins, but He graciously pardoned me with His forgiveness and did not punish me."

al-Dahhak said: Every "zann" (thought/supposition) in the Qur'an from a believer is certainty (yaqin), and from an unbeliever it is doubt (shakk).

Mujahid said: The thought of the Hereafter is certainty, and the thought of this world is doubt.

al-Hasan said concerning this verse: The believer thought well of his Lord, so he did good deeds for the Hereafter, and the unbeliever thought ill of his Lord, so he did evil deeds.

It is said: The expression "thought" (zann) here is to indicate that what passes through the self of thoughts, which theoretical sciences generally do not escape, does not harm belief.

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾, i.e., in a praiseworthy life, not a disliked one, or one possessing contentment, i.e., its owner is content with it.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: "radiyah" means "marḍiyyah" (pleasing), like His saying: ﴿of a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 6], i.e., "mudfuq" (gushed). Thus what belongs to its owner is attributed to the life, and this is metaphor (majaz) in attribution.

﴿In a lofty garden﴾, i.e., elevated in place because it is in the heaven, or elevated in its dwellings, or great in souls.

﴿Its clusters are near﴾. "Qutuf" is the plural of "qitf" with a kasra on the qaf, meaning what is plucked from fruits; "qatf" with a fatha is the verbal noun, and "qataf" with a fatha or kasra is the time of plucking. The meaning is that its fruits are close to whoever reaches for them, whether standing, sitting, or lying down.

﴿"Eat and drink"﴾, i.e., it will be said to them in the Garden: "Eat and drink, with relish (hanian)," i.e., eating and drinking without any turbidity or disturbance. ﴿For what you sent forward in the past days﴾, i.e., because of the righteous deeds you put forward in the world.

Mujahid said: They are the days of fasting. As for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say, in grief and distress, because of what he sees in it of his evil deeds:

﴿"Oh, I wish I had not been given my record!"﴾, i.e., I wish I had not been given my record.

﴿"And I had not known what my reckoning is!"﴾, i.e., I did not know what my reckoning is, because all of it is against him.

﴿"Oh, I wish it had been the decisive end!"﴾, i.e., I wish the death I died had been the decisive one, and I had not been raised after it. The meaning of "al-qadiyah" is the one that cuts off life. The meaning is that he wishes for the permanence of death and the non-resurrection, when he witnesses the evil of his deeds and the punishment to which he will go. So the pronoun in "layta-ha" refers to the death he had died, though it is not mentioned, because, being so evident, it is as if it had been mentioned.

Qatadah said: He wished for death, and there was nothing in the world more hateful to him than it; and worse than death is that for which one seeks death.

It is also said: The pronoun refers to the state he witnessed upon reading the Book; the meaning: "Oh, I wish this state had been the death that was decreed upon me."

﴿"My wealth has not availed me"﴾, i.e., it did not repel from me any of Allah's punishment, whether "ma" is negative or interrogative; the meaning being: "What did my wealth avail me?"

﴿"My authority has perished from me"﴾, i.e., my proof has perished from me and gone astray from me. So said Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, and al-Dahhak.

Ibn Zayd said: It means my authority in the world, which is kingship. It was also said: my dominance over my limbs.

Muqatil said: It means when the limbs testified against him with polytheism.

And then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿"Seize him and shackle him"﴾, i.e., gather his hand to his neck with shackles.

﴿"Then burn him in the Blazing Fire"﴾, i.e., cause him to enter the Blazing Fire. The meaning is: do not burn him except in the Blazing Fire, which is the great fire.

﴿"Then insert him into a chain whose length is seventy cubits"﴾. The "silsilah" is a chain of linked rings, and its "dar'" (length) is its extent.

al-Hasan said: Allah knows with which cubit it is measured.

Nawf al-Shami said: Each cubit is seventy spans (ba'), and each span is farther than the distance between you and Makkah. Nawf was in the courtyard (rahbah) of Kufah.

Muqatil said: If one of its links were placed on the peak of a mountain, it would melt as lead melts. The meaning of "fasluk-uh" is "make him enter it," as one says "salaktuhu al-tariq," when one causes him to enter the road.

Sufyan said: We have been told that it enters through his rear until it comes out of his mouth.

al-Kalbi said: It threads him as a thread goes through pearls.

Suwayd ibn Abi Najih said: I have been told that all the people of the Fire are in that chain. The placing of the chain first is to indicate exclusivity, like the placing of the Blazing Fire.

The clause ﴿"Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty"﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) of what precedes it.

﴿"And did not urge the feeding of the needy"﴾, i.e., he did not urge feeding the needy from his wealth, or he did not urge others to feed them. The word "ta'am" (food) is placed in the position of "ik'am" (feeding), just as "'ata'" (gift) is placed in the position of "i'ta'" (giving), as the poet said:

"Kafran ba'da radd mawti 'anni wa ba'da 'ata'ika al-mal al-ri'aba?"
(Is it disbelief after my death was averted from me, and after your giving of abundant wealth?)

That is, after your giving. Abu 'Ubayd, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-Darda' that he said: "Allah has a chain from which the cauldrons of the Fire have continued to boil since Allah created Hell until the Day it is placed around the necks of people. Allah has saved us from half of it through our faith in Allah, the Mighty. So feed the poor, O Umm al-Darda'."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the route of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Ghislin is the blood, the water and the pus that flows from their flesh."

al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "If a bucket of ghislin were poured out in this world, it would make the people of this world stink."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Ghislin is the name of a food of the people of the Fire."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him concerning ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾ that he said: "By what you see and what you do not see."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ that he said: "By power."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "The jugular (al-watayn) is the vein of the heart."

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated from him as well that he said: "The jugular is the nияt of the heart." (p. 1528)

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from him as well that he said: "It is the cord of the heart that is in the back."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 69, verse 19–52 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glorified be He, mentioned the Reckoning (al-'ard), He mentioned what will happen in it, so He said: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾, i.e., he is given his record which the scribes (al-hafaza) wrote down of his deeds, ﴿he will say, "Here, read my record!"﴾ He says this out of joy and delight.

Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Kisa'i said: The Arabs say: "ha, ya rajul" (hā, O man); for two it is "hā'uma, ya rajulan"; for the plural it is "hā'um, ya rijal" (O men). It is said that the original was "hā'ukum," and the hamza replaced the kaf. Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of "hā'um" is "come here" (ta'ālaw).

Muqatil said: it means "halumma" (come), and it was said: "take" (khudhu). It is an ism fi'l (verb-noun), though it may be a plain verb when the attached pronouns of the plural subject are joined to it. It has three dialectal forms, as is known in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis). His saying "kitabiyah" is the object of "iqra'u" (read), because it is the nearer of the two verbs, and the object of "hā'um" is omitted, indicated by the object of "iqra'u." The estimated sense is: "Hā'um kitabiyah, iqra'u kitabiyah." The ha' in "kitabiyah," "hisabiyah," "sultaniyah," and "maliyah" is the ha' al-sakt (the pausal ha').

The majority (al-Jumhur) read these with the ha' kept both in pause and in continuous recitation, in conformity with the orthography of the Mushaf. Were it not for this, it would be dropped in continuous recitation, as is the case with the ha' al-sakt. Abu 'Ubayd preferred to deliberately pause on it, so as to agree with the language in attaching the ha' for pausing, and to agree with the script, meaning the script of the Mushaf. (p-1526)

Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Humayd, Mujahid, al-A'mash, and Ya'qub read it with the ha' omitted in continuous recitation and kept in pause, in all these words.

This reading is also transmitted from Hamzah, and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, following the language.

It is narrated from Ibn Muhaysin that he read it with the ha' omitted both in continuous recitation and in pause.

﴿Indeed, I thought that I would meet my reckoning﴾, i.e., I knew and was certain in the world that I would be called to account in the Hereafter. It was also said: the meaning is: "I thought that Allah would seize me for my sins, but He graciously pardoned me with His forgiveness and did not punish me."

al-Dahhak said: Every "zann" (thought/supposition) in the Qur'an from a believer is certainty (yaqin), and from an unbeliever it is doubt (shakk).

Mujahid said: The thought of the Hereafter is certainty, and the thought of this world is doubt.

al-Hasan said concerning this verse: The believer thought well of his Lord, so he did good deeds for the Hereafter, and the unbeliever thought ill of his Lord, so he did evil deeds.

It is said: The expression "thought" (zann) here is to indicate that what passes through the self of thoughts, which theoretical sciences generally do not escape, does not harm belief.

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾, i.e., in a praiseworthy life, not a disliked one, or one possessing contentment, i.e., its owner is content with it.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: "radiyah" means "marḍiyyah" (pleasing), like His saying: ﴿of a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 6], i.e., "mudfuq" (gushed). Thus what belongs to its owner is attributed to the life, and this is metaphor (majaz) in attribution.

﴿In a lofty garden﴾, i.e., elevated in place because it is in the heaven, or elevated in its dwellings, or great in souls.

﴿Its clusters are near﴾. "Qutuf" is the plural of "qitf" with a kasra on the qaf, meaning what is plucked from fruits; "qatf" with a fatha is the verbal noun, and "qataf" with a fatha or kasra is the time of plucking. The meaning is that its fruits are close to whoever reaches for them, whether standing, sitting, or lying down.

﴿"Eat and drink"﴾, i.e., it will be said to them in the Garden: "Eat and drink, with relish (hanian)," i.e., eating and drinking without any turbidity or disturbance. ﴿For what you sent forward in the past days﴾, i.e., because of the righteous deeds you put forward in the world.

Mujahid said: They are the days of fasting. As for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say, in grief and distress, because of what he sees in it of his evil deeds:

﴿"Oh, I wish I had not been given my record!"﴾, i.e., I wish I had not been given my record.

﴿"And I had not known what my reckoning is!"﴾, i.e., I did not know what my reckoning is, because all of it is against him.

﴿"Oh, I wish it had been the decisive end!"﴾, i.e., I wish the death I died had been the decisive one, and I had not been raised after it. The meaning of "al-qadiyah" is the one that cuts off life. The meaning is that he wishes for the permanence of death and the non-resurrection, when he witnesses the evil of his deeds and the punishment to which he will go. So the pronoun in "layta-ha" refers to the death he had died, though it is not mentioned, because, being so evident, it is as if it had been mentioned.

Qatadah said: He wished for death, and there was nothing in the world more hateful to him than it; and worse than death is that for which one seeks death.

It is also said: The pronoun refers to the state he witnessed upon reading the Book; the meaning: "Oh, I wish this state had been the death that was decreed upon me."

﴿"My wealth has not availed me"﴾, i.e., it did not repel from me any of Allah's punishment, whether "ma" is negative or interrogative; the meaning being: "What did my wealth avail me?"

﴿"My authority has perished from me"﴾, i.e., my proof has perished from me and gone astray from me. So said Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, and al-Dahhak.

Ibn Zayd said: It means my authority in the world, which is kingship. It was also said: my dominance over my limbs.

Muqatil said: It means when the limbs testified against him with polytheism.

And then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿"Seize him and shackle him"﴾, i.e., gather his hand to his neck with shackles.

﴿"Then burn him in the Blazing Fire"﴾, i.e., cause him to enter the Blazing Fire. The meaning is: do not burn him except in the Blazing Fire, which is the great fire.

﴿"Then insert him into a chain whose length is seventy cubits"﴾. The "silsilah" is a chain of linked rings, and its "dar'" (length) is its extent.

al-Hasan said: Allah knows with which cubit it is measured.

Nawf al-Shami said: Each cubit is seventy spans (ba'), and each span is farther than the distance between you and Makkah. Nawf was in the courtyard (rahbah) of Kufah.

Muqatil said: If one of its links were placed on the peak of a mountain, it would melt as lead melts. The meaning of "fasluk-uh" is "make him enter it," as one says "salaktuhu al-tariq," when one causes him to enter the road.

Sufyan said: We have been told that it enters through his rear until it comes out of his mouth.

al-Kalbi said: It threads him as a thread goes through pearls.

Suwayd ibn Abi Najih said: I have been told that all the people of the Fire are in that chain. The placing of the chain first is to indicate exclusivity, like the placing of the Blazing Fire.

The clause ﴿"Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty"﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) of what precedes it.

﴿"And did not urge the feeding of the needy"﴾, i.e., he did not urge feeding the needy from his wealth, or he did not urge others to feed them. The word "ta'am" (food) is placed in the position of "ik'am" (feeding), just as "'ata'" (gift) is placed in the position of "i'ta'" (giving), as the poet said:

"Kafran ba'da radd mawti 'anni wa ba'da 'ata'ika al-mal al-ri'aba?"
(Is it disbelief after my death was averted from me, and after your giving of abundant wealth?)

That is, after your giving. It is also permissible that "ta'am" retain its own meaning, not being placed in the position of the verbal noun, and the meaning is: he does not urge himself or others to give the very food of the needy. In making this the companion of abandoning belief in Allah, there is an exhortation to give charity to the needy and to meet their need, and an urging of oneself and people to that, which shows, in the most eloquent way and conveying the most complete benefit, that withholding it is among the greatest crimes and gravest sins.

﴿So there is not for him today here any close friend﴾, i.e., there will be no close relative for him on the Day of Resurrection in the Hereafter who benefits him or intercedes for him, because it is a day on which one flees from his close relative, and the beloved runs from his beloved.

﴿Nor any food except from ghislin﴾, i.e., he has no food to eat except the pus of the people of the Fire and what flows from their bodies of discharge and pus. "Ghislin" is "fi'lin" from "ghasl" (washing).

al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: It is a tree that the people of the Fire eat.

Qatadah said: It is the worst of foods.

Ibn Zayd said: No one knows what it is, nor what the zaqqum is, except Allah, Most High.

He, glorified be He, said in another place: ﴿They have no food except from *dari'*﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6]. So it is possible that *dari'* is *ghislin*. It was also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the meaning is: "So there is not for him today here any close friend except from ghislin," the *hamim* being boiling water. "Nor any food" means: they have no food they eat. There is no necessity for this inversion.

The clause ﴿"which none eat except the sinners"﴾ is an attribute of *ghislin*, and what is meant is the possessors of sins and the lords of transgressions.

al-Kalbi said: What is meant is polytheism.

The majority read *al-khati'un* with hamza, which is the active participle of *khati'a*, meaning one who does what is not right deliberately, while *al-mukhti'* is one who does it unintentionally.

al-Zuhri, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and al-Hasan read *al-khatiyun* with a damma on the *ya'* in place of the hamza.

Nafi' in one transmission read it with a damma on the *ta'* without hamza.

﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾. This is a rebuttal of the speech of the polytheists, as if He said: "The matter is not as you say," and "la" is extra (za'idah), the estimated sense being: "So I swear by what you witness and what you do not witness."

Qatadah said: He swore by all things, what is seen of them and what is not seen, so this includes all created beings. It was also said: "la" is not extra, but is for negating the oath, i.e., "I have no need of an oath because the truth in this is clear." The first view is preferred.

﴿Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger﴾, i.e., the Qur'an is indeed the recitation of a noble Messenger, with the meaning of "Messenger" being Muhammad ﷺ, or it is a speech conveyed by a noble Messenger.

al-Hasan, al-Kalbi, and Muqatil said: He means by it Jibril, and the evidence is His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger, possessor of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne﴾ [al-Takwir: 19–20]. In any case, the Qur'an is not the speech of Muhammad ﷺ, nor the speech of Jibril (peace be upon him), but it is the speech of Allah, so the estimation of "recitation" or "conveyance" is necessary.

﴿Nor is it the speech of a poet﴾, as you claim, because it is not among the kinds of poetry nor similar to it. ﴿Little is it that you believe﴾, i.e., you believe with little belief and confirm with slight confirmation, and "ma" is extra.

﴿Nor the speech of a soothsayer﴾, as you claim, for soothsaying is another matter with no common link between it and this. ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾, i.e., you remember a little, or you remember for a short time, and "ma" is extra. The paucity in both places is in the sense of negation, i.e., you do not believe and you do not remember at all.

﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. The majority read it in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is a revelation." Abu al-Sammak read it in the accusative as a verbal noun, with a verb omitted, i.e., "it was revealed as a revelation," and the meaning: "Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger, and it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds upon his tongue."

﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾, i.e., if that Messenger, who is Muhammad, or Jibril as previously mentioned, had fabricated. "Taqawwul" is the forced making of speech, and the meaning is: if he had forced that and brought it from his own self. Lying is called "taqawwul" because it is forced speech, and every liar forces what he lies about.

The majority read *taqawwala* in the active voice.

It is also read in the passive voice with *ba'd* in the nominative.

Ibn Dhakwan read *wa-law yaqul* in the imperfect form. *Al-aqawil* is the plural of *aqwal*, and *aqwal* is the plural of *qawl*.

﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾, i.e., by his right hand. Ibn Jarir said: This speech came in the manner of humiliation, according to the custom of people in seizing the one who is to be punished.

al-Farra', al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutaybah said: ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ means: with power and might. Ibn Qutaybah said: He placed the right hand in the position of power, because the strength of everything is in its right side, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Idha ma rayatun nusibat li-majdin, talaqqaha 'arabatu bi-l-yamin"
(When a banner is raised for glory, 'Arabah receives it with the right hand.)

And the saying of another:

"Wa lamma ra'aytu al-shams ashraqa nuruha, tanawaltu minha hajati bi-yamini"
(When I saw the sun shine its light, I took from it my need with my right hand.)

﴿Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾. The "watin" is a vein running along the back until it reaches the heart, and this is a depiction of his destruction in the most dreadful manner kings inflict on those they are angry with.

al-Wahidi said: The commentators say it is the nerve of the heart (niyat al-qalb). End of quotation. From this is the poet's saying:

"Idha ballaghtini wa hamalti rahli 'arabata fashriqi bi-dami al-watin"
(When you bring me and carry my saddle to 'Arabah, then choke on the blood of the aorta.)

﴿So none of you could prevent Us from him﴾, i.e., none of you would restrain Us from him or repel Us from him. So how would he fabricate lies against Allah for your sake, knowing that if he did so We would punish him, and you could not repel or restrain Us from him? "Hajizin" is an attribute of "ahad" (one), or the predicate of the Hijazi "ma."

﴿And indeed, it is a source of anguish for the disbelievers.﴾ That is: the Qur'an will be a source of regret and remorse for the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the reward of the believers. It was also said: it is their anguish in this world when they could not oppose it when they were challenged to produce a surah like it.

﴿And indeed, it is the certain truth.﴾ That is: the Qur'an, because it is from Allah, is true; so no doubt surrounds it, and no uncertainty reaches it.

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ That is: declare Him far above what does not befit Him. It was also said: pray to your Lord. The first is more appropriate.

And then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿"Seize him and shackle him"﴾, i.e., gather his hand to his neck with shackles.

﴿"Then burn him in the Blazing Fire"﴾, i.e., cause him to enter the Blazing Fire. The meaning is: do not burn him except in the Blazing Fire, which is the great fire.

﴿"Then insert him into a chain whose length is seventy cubits"﴾. The "silsilah" is a chain of linked rings, and its "dar'" (length) is its extent.

al-Hasan said: Allah knows with which cubit it is measured.

Nawf al-Shami said: Each cubit is seventy spans (ba'), and each span is farther than the distance between you and Makkah. Nawf was in the courtyard (rahbah) of Kufah.

Muqatil said: If one of its links were placed on the peak of a mountain, it would melt as lead melts. The meaning of "fasluk-uh" is "make him enter it," as one says "salaktuhu al-tariq," when one causes him to enter the road.

Sufyan said: We have been told that it enters through his rear until it comes out of his mouth.

al-Kalbi said: It threads him as a thread goes through pearls.

Suwayd ibn Abi Najih said: I have been told that all the people of the Fire are in that chain. The placing of the chain first is to indicate exclusivity, like the placing of the Blazing Fire.

The clause ﴿"Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty"﴾ is an explanation (ta'lil) of what precedes it.

﴿"And did not urge the feeding of the needy"﴾, i.e., he did not urge feeding the needy from his wealth, or he did not urge others to feed them. The word "ta'am" (food) is placed in the position of "ik'am" (feeding), just as "'ata'" (gift) is placed in the position of "i'ta'" (giving), as the poet said:

"Kafran ba'da radd mawti 'anni wa ba'da 'ata'ika al-mal al-ri'aba?"
(Is it disbelief after my death was averted from me, and after your giving of abundant wealth?)

That is, after your giving. It is also permissible that "ta'am" retain its own meaning, not being placed in the position of the verbal noun, and the meaning is: he does not urge himself or others to give the very food of the needy. In making this the companion of abandoning belief in Allah, there is an exhortation to give charity to the needy and to meet their need, and an urging of oneself and people to that, which shows, in the most eloquent way and conveying the most complete benefit, that withholding it is among the greatest crimes and gravest sins.

﴿So there is not for him today here any close friend﴾, i.e., there will be no close relative for him on the Day of Resurrection in the Hereafter who benefits him or intercedes for him, because it is a day on which one flees from his close relative, and the beloved runs from his beloved.

﴿Nor any food except from ghislin﴾, i.e., he has no food to eat except the pus of the people of the Fire and what flows from their bodies of discharge and pus. "Ghislin" is "fi'lin" from "ghasl" (washing).

al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: It is a tree that the people of the Fire eat.

Qatadah said: It is the worst of foods.

Ibn Zayd said: No one knows what it is, nor what the zaqqum is, except Allah, Most High.

He, glorified be He, said in another place: ﴿They have no food except from *dari'*﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6]. So it is possible that *dari'* is *ghislin*. It was also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, and the meaning is: "So there is not for him today here any close friend except from ghislin," the *hamim* being boiling water. "Nor any food" means: they have no food they eat. There is no necessity for this inversion.

The clause ﴿"which none eat except the sinners"﴾ is an attribute of *ghislin*, and what is meant is the possessors of sins and the lords of transgressions.

al-Kalbi said: What is meant is polytheism.

The majority read *al-khati'un* with hamza, which is the active participle of *khati'a*, meaning one who does what is not right deliberately, while *al-mukhti'* is one who does it unintentionally.

al-Zuhri, Talhah ibn Musarrif, and al-Hasan read *al-khatiyun* with a damma on the *ya'* in place of the hamza.

Nafi' in one transmission read it with a damma on the *ta'* without hamza.

﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾. This is a rebuttal of the speech of the polytheists, as if He said: "The matter is not as you say," and "la" is extra (za'idah), the estimated sense being: "So I swear by what you witness and what you do not witness."

Qatadah said: He swore by all things, what is seen of them and what is not seen, so this includes all created beings. It was also said: "la" is not extra, but is for negating the oath, i.e., "I have no need of an oath because the truth in this is clear." The first view is preferred.

﴿Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger﴾, i.e., the Qur'an is indeed the recitation of a noble Messenger, with the meaning of "Messenger" being Muhammad ﷺ, or it is a speech conveyed by a noble Messenger.

al-Hasan, al-Kalbi, and Muqatil said: He means by it Jibril, and the evidence is His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger, possessor of power, with esteem near the Owner of the Throne﴾ [al-Takwir: 19–20]. In any case, the Qur'an is not the speech of Muhammad ﷺ, nor the speech of Jibril (peace be upon him), but it is the speech of Allah, so the estimation of "recitation" or "conveyance" is necessary.

﴿Nor is it the speech of a poet﴾, as you claim, because it is not among the kinds of poetry nor similar to it. ﴿Little is it that you believe﴾, i.e., you believe with little belief and confirm with slight confirmation, and "ma" is extra.

﴿Nor the speech of a soothsayer﴾, as you claim, for soothsaying is another matter with no common link between it and this. ﴿Little is it that you remember﴾, i.e., you remember a little, or you remember for a short time, and "ma" is extra. The paucity in both places is in the sense of negation, i.e., you do not believe and you do not remember at all.

﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾. The majority read it in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "it is a revelation." Abu al-Sammak read it in the accusative as a verbal noun, with a verb omitted, i.e., "it was revealed as a revelation," and the meaning: "Indeed, it is the speech of a noble Messenger, and it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds upon his tongue."

﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾, i.e., if that Messenger, who is Muhammad, or Jibril as previously mentioned, had fabricated. "Taqawwul" is the forced making of speech, and the meaning is: if he had forced that and brought it from his own self. Lying is called "taqawwul" because it is forced speech, and every liar forces what he lies about.

The majority read *taqawwala* in the active voice.

It is also read in the passive voice with *ba'd* in the nominative.

Ibn Dhakwan read *wa-law yaqul* in the imperfect form. *Al-aqawil* is the plural of *aqwal*, and *aqwal* is the plural of *qawl*.

﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾, i.e., by his right hand. Ibn Jarir said: This speech came in the manner of humiliation, according to the custom of people in seizing the one who is to be punished.

al-Farra', al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutaybah said: ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ means: with power and might. Ibn Qutaybah said: He placed the right hand in the position of power, because the strength of everything is in its right side, and from this is the poet's saying:

"Idha ma rayatun nusibat li-majdin, talaqqaha 'arabatu bi-l-yamin"
(When a banner is raised for glory, 'Arabah receives it with the right hand.)

And the saying of another:

"Wa lamma ra'aytu al-shams ashraqa nuruha, tanawaltu minha hajati bi-yamini"
(When I saw the sun shine its light, I took from it my need with my right hand.)

﴿Then We would have cut from him the aorta﴾. The "watin" is a vein running along the back until it reaches the heart, and this is a depiction of his destruction in the most dreadful manner kings inflict on those they are angry with.

al-Wahidi said: The commentators say it is the nerve of the heart (niyat al-qalb). End of quotation. From this is the poet's saying:

"Idha ballaghtini wa hamalti rahli 'arabata fashriqi bi-dami al-watin"
(When you bring me and carry my saddle to 'Arabah, then choke on the blood of the aorta.)

﴿So none of you could prevent Us from him﴾, i.e., none of you would restrain Us from him or repel Us from him. So how would he fabricate lies against Allah for your sake, knowing that if he did so We would punish him, and you could not repel or restrain Us from him? "Hajizin" is an attribute of "ahad" (one), or the predicate of the Hijazi "ma."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 69, verses 19–52 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for the God-fearing.﴾ That is: the Qur'an is a reminder for the people of taqwa (God-consciousness), because they are the ones who benefit from it.

﴿And indeed, We know that among you are deniers.﴾ That is: some of you deny the Qur'an, and We will requite them for that. In this there is a severe warning.

﴿And indeed, it is a source of anguish for the disbelievers.﴾ That is: the Qur'an will be a source of regret and remorse for the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the reward of the believers. It was also said: it is their anguish in this world when they could not oppose it when they were challenged to produce a surah like it.

﴿And indeed, it is the certain truth.﴾ That is: the Qur'an, because it is from Allah, is true; so no doubt surrounds it, and no uncertainty reaches it.

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾ That is: declare Him far above what does not befit Him. It was also said: pray to your Lord. The first is more appropriate.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Indeed, I thought﴾ that he said: "I was certain."

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib concerning ﴿its fruits are near at hand﴾ that he said: "close."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Bara' concerning the verse that he said: "A man will take of its fruits while standing."

Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿Then bind him﴾ that he said: "The chain enters his backside and comes out from his mouth, then they are strung on it as locusts are strung on a stick and then roasted."

Abu 'Ubayd, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abu al-Darda' that he said: "Allah has a chain from which the cauldrons of the Fire have continued to boil since Allah created Hell until the Day it is placed around the necks of people. Allah has saved us from half of it through our faith in Allah, the Mighty. So feed the poor, O Umm al-Darda'."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated through the route of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Ghislin is the blood, the water and the pus that flows from their flesh."

al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "If a bucket of ghislin were poured out in this world, it would make the people of this world stink."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Ghislin is the name of a food of the people of the Fire."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him concerning ﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾ that he said: "By what you see and what you do not see."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ that he said: "By power."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him that he said: "The jugular (al-watayn) is the vein of the heart."

al-Firyabi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated from him as well that he said: "The jugular is the nияt of the heart." (p. 1528)

Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from him as well that he said: "It is the cord of the heart that is in the back."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 69, verse 19–52 (part 1 of 2):

When He, glorified be He, mentioned the Reckoning (al-'ard), He mentioned what will happen in it, so He said: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾, i.e., he is given his record which the scribes (al-hafaza) wrote down of his deeds, ﴿he will say, "Here, read my record!"﴾ He says this out of joy and delight.

Ibn al-Sikkit and al-Kisa'i said: The Arabs say: "ha, ya rajul" (hā, O man); for two it is "hā'uma, ya rajulan"; for the plural it is "hā'um, ya rijal" (O men). It is said that the original was "hā'ukum," and the hamza replaced the kaf. Ibn Zayd said: The meaning of "hā'um" is "come here" (ta'ālaw).

Muqatil said: it means "halumma" (come), and it was said: "take" (khudhu). It is an ism fi'l (verb-noun), though it may be a plain verb when the attached pronouns of the plural subject are joined to it. It has three dialectal forms, as is known in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis). His saying "kitabiyah" is the object of "iqra'u" (read), because it is the nearer of the two verbs, and the object of "hā'um" is omitted, indicated by the object of "iqra'u." The estimated sense is: "Hā'um kitabiyah, iqra'u kitabiyah." The ha' in "kitabiyah," "hisabiyah," "sultaniyah," and "maliyah" is the ha' al-sakt (the pausal ha').

The majority (al-Jumhur) read these with the ha' kept both in pause and in continuous recitation, in conformity with the orthography of the Mushaf. Were it not for this, it would be dropped in continuous recitation, as is the case with the ha' al-sakt. Abu 'Ubayd preferred to deliberately pause on it, so as to agree with the language in attaching the ha' for pausing, and to agree with the script, meaning the script of the Mushaf. (p-1526)

Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Humayd, Mujahid, al-A'mash, and Ya'qub read it with the ha' omitted in continuous recitation and kept in pause, in all these words.

This reading is also transmitted from Hamzah, and Abu Hatim preferred this reading, following the language.

It is narrated from Ibn Muhaysin that he read it with the ha' omitted both in continuous recitation and in pause.

﴿Indeed, I thought that I would meet my reckoning﴾, i.e., I knew and was certain in the world that I would be called to account in the Hereafter. It was also said: the meaning is: "I thought that Allah would seize me for my sins, but He graciously pardoned me with His forgiveness and did not punish me."

al-Dahhak said: Every "zann" (thought/supposition) in the Qur'an from a believer is certainty (yaqin), and from an unbeliever it is doubt (shakk).

Mujahid said: The thought of the Hereafter is certainty, and the thought of this world is doubt.

al-Hasan said concerning this verse: The believer thought well of his Lord, so he did good deeds for the Hereafter, and the unbeliever thought ill of his Lord, so he did evil deeds.

It is said: The expression "thought" (zann) here is to indicate that what passes through the self of thoughts, which theoretical sciences generally do not escape, does not harm belief.

﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾, i.e., in a praiseworthy life, not a disliked one, or one possessing contentment, i.e., its owner is content with it.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Farra' said: "radiyah" means "marḍiyyah" (pleasing), like His saying: ﴿of a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 6], i.e., "mudfuq" (gushed). Thus what belongs to its owner is attributed to the life, and this is metaphor (majaz) in attribution.

﴿In a lofty garden﴾, i.e., elevated in place because it is in the heaven, or elevated in its dwellings, or great in souls.

﴿Its clusters are near﴾. "Qutuf" is the plural of "qitf" with a kasra on the qaf, meaning what is plucked from fruits; "qatf" with a fatha is the verbal noun, and "qataf" with a fatha or kasra is the time of plucking. The meaning is that its fruits are close to whoever reaches for them, whether standing, sitting, or lying down.

﴿"Eat and drink"﴾, i.e., it will be said to them in the Garden: "Eat and drink, with relish (hanian)," i.e., eating and drinking without any turbidity or disturbance. ﴿For what you sent forward in the past days﴾, i.e., because of the righteous deeds you put forward in the world.

Mujahid said: They are the days of fasting. As for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say, in grief and distress, because of what he sees in it of his evil deeds:

﴿"Oh, I wish I had not been given my record!"﴾, i.e., I wish I had not been given my record.

﴿"And I had not known what my reckoning is!"﴾, i.e., I did not know what my reckoning is, because all of it is against him.

﴿"Oh, I wish it had been the decisive end!"﴾, i.e., I wish the death I died had been the decisive one, and I had not been raised after it. The meaning of "al-qadiyah" is the one that cuts off life. The meaning is that he wishes for the permanence of death and the non-resurrection, when he witnesses the evil of his deeds and the punishment to which he will go. So the pronoun in "layta-ha" refers to the death he had died, though it is not mentioned, because, being so evident, it is as if it had been mentioned.

Qatadah said: He wished for death, and there was nothing in the world more hateful to him than it; and worse than death is that for which one seeks death.

It is also said: The pronoun refers to the state he witnessed upon reading the Book; the meaning: "Oh, I wish this state had been the death that was decreed upon me."

﴿"My wealth has not availed me"﴾, i.e., it did not repel from me any of Allah's punishment, whether "ma" is negative or interrogative; the meaning being: "What did my wealth avail me?"

﴿"My authority has perished from me"﴾, i.e., my proof has perished from me and gone astray from me. So said Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, and al-Dahhak.

Ibn Zayd said: It means my authority in the world, which is kingship. It was also said: my dominance over my limbs.

Muqatil said: It means when the limbs testified against him with polytheism.
